analysis.one_liner: Requires online platforms to tell users what data they collect, honor opt-outs, and report data breaches within 72 hours.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to; it received no hearing, no vote, and expired at the end of 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required websites and apps — social networks, search engines, email services, ad networks — to tell users up front that their personal data will be collected and shared, and let users refuse that collection. Platforms would have to hand users a free copy of their own data, delete data soon after an account closes, and notify users within 72 hours of a data breach. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules; violations would count as unfair or deceptive practices under FTC law.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of Americans who use social media, search engines, email, and other online services. They would gain the right to see what data companies hold about them, learn who it was sold to, opt out of collection, and be told quickly when their data leaks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of social media and online platforms

how_it_helps.text: Before creating an account, a user must be told that their personal data — including location, messages, health information, and financial details — will be collected and used by the platform and third parties, and given the option to prohibit it [S3].
Platforms must give users a free, electronic copy of the personal data they have processed, including a list of everyone who received that data through sale or otherwise [S3].

Operators must notify a user within 72 hours of learning their data was transmitted in violation of the platform's privacy program, and offer the user the option to erase their data, stop further sharing, or close the account [S3].
Personal data must become inaccessible within 30 days after a user closes an account, and users must be able to withdraw consent as easily as they gave it [S3].
Violations count as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act, and the FTC gains authority over common carriers (large telecom companies currently exempt from FTC enforcement) and nonprofits [S2].
State attorneys general may sue violators in federal court on behalf of their residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms and the advertising-data industry, which profit from collecting and selling user data. They would bear compliance costs — privacy programs, audits every two years, disclosure and opt-out systems — and lose some ability to monetize data from users who opt out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech platforms and the ad-data industry

drawbacks.text: If a user's opt-out of data collection would make the platform inoperable, the operator may deny that user certain services or deny access entirely — meaning users could face a take-it-or-leave-it choice between their privacy and using the service [S3].

The bill creates no private right of action: individual users cannot sue on their own; enforcement rests entirely with the FTC and state attorneys general, who must prioritize which cases to pursue [S3].

Compliance costs fall on every covered platform, including small websites and apps, and the definition of covered platforms is broad enough to include search engines, email services, and internet providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The user rights are real — data access, breach notification, and deletion after account closure address practices most users cannot see or control today. But the design has two significant weaknesses: the inoperability loophole lets platforms pressure users into consenting, and ordinary people have no individual right to sue. The bill would have shifted meaningful power toward users, though less decisively than stricter privacy laws would have.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, joined by Senators Kennedy (R-LA), Manchin (D-WV), and Burr (R-NC) as original cosponsors [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
Three senators cosponsored the bill: two Republicans and one Democrat [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and the ad-data industry are better off: they continue collecting and monetizing user data with no federal notice, opt-out, breach-notification, or data-access requirements. Users' data remains available to companies under the same rules as before.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four original backers split evenly between the parties — two Democrats and two Republicans — and its three added cosponsors were two Republicans and one Democrat, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists of how the parties stood.

industries.industry: Online platforms and social media companies
industries.note: They would face mandatory disclosure, opt-out elections, user data access, deletion after account closure, and FTC enforcement — costs and constraints on practices that currently generate advertising revenue. Their gain from the bill's death is that data collection continues unrestricted.
The bill requires platforms to tell users exactly who received their data through sale, and lets users prohibit collection — shrinking the pool of data available to be bought and sold.
Common carriers are currently exempt from FTC enforcement; the bill would have put them under FTC privacy enforcement for the first time.
